query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Systematic removal of one or more elements from the equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy alters the local chemical interactions that control both lattice distortion/staking fault energy and the propensity for a dislocation‐triggered fcc‐to‐hcp transformation. In particular, eliminating Mn reduces magnetic frustration, which in turn lowers the energetic barrier for localized phase transformation at stacking faults and twin boundaries. This combined modification of local lattice conditions and transformation capacity modulates dislocation mobility and work hardening during deformation, leading to measurable differences in strength and ductility compared to the quinary baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single‐phase FCC alloys obtained via identical thermomechanical processing, including the quinary Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy and its derived quaternary/ternary subsets (e.g. Cr–Co–Ni or similar systems).
generation.intervention: Systematically remove one or two elements (e.g. Mn) from the quinary alloy while ensuring all compositions retain a single‐phase FCC microstructure after identical processing.
generation.conditions: Ambient (or room/cryogenic) temperature uniaxial tensile deformation with controlled strain rate and identical sample processing to ensure comparable grain size, defect density, and phase stability across the alloy variants.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and stacking fault energies that regulate dislocation slip, along with the emergence of nanoscale hcp regions at defect sites.
generation.mechanism: Removal of elements such as Mn changes the balance of atomic size differences and electronic/magnetic interactions, thereby reducing lattice distortion and magnetic frustration. This permits a greater likelihood of a deformation‐induced fcc‐to‐hcp transformation at stacking faults and twin boundaries. The resulting nanoscale hcp regions serve as additional obstacles to dislocation motion, enhancing strain hardening and modifying yield behavior relative to the parent quinary alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni baseline, alloys with reduced constituent count (e.g. Mn‐free ternary/quaternary compositions) are expected to exhibit altered yield strength and work hardening behavior – specifically, an increased propensity for localized hcp phase formation at defects that correlates with enhanced strain hardening and ductility, provided that the transformation mechanism dominates over any loss in lattice distortion-induced strengthening.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy processed under identical thermomechanical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to alloys that maintain a single-phase FCC structure following identical thermomechanical processing and that are deformed under controlled temperature and strain rate conditions. It may not hold if additional phases form or if processing conditions lead to significant microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.uncertainty: The balance between the effects of reduced lattice distortion (which might weaken strengthening) and the beneficial impact of an enabled fcc‐to‐hcp transformation (which may enhance strain hardening) remains to be quantified. The net mechanical response may depend sensitively on processing details and the relative influence of magnetic interactions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate the equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy alongside its reduced-element derivatives (e.g. a Mn-free ternary or quaternary alloy) using identical thermomechanical processing to ensure a single-phase FCC structure. Subject all alloys to controlled uniaxial tensile tests at the same temperature and strain rate. Use in situ high-resolution TEM and diffraction techniques to quantify both local lattice distortions and the formation of nanoscale hcp regions during deformation.
measurements: Yield strength and work hardening rate from stress–strain curves
Fraction and spatial distribution of deformation-induced hcp phase (via TEM/XRD)
Indicators of local lattice distortion and stacking fault energy variations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduced-element alloys do not exhibit a significantly higher fraction of deformation-induced hcp phase or if their mechanical properties (e.g. yield strength, strain hardening, and ductility) do not systematically diverge from those of the quinary baseline as predicted – particularly if no correlation is observed between local structural mediators and mechanical performance – then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr). cited_evidence.text: We have shown the existence of a nanostructure with hcp phase in the equiatomic CrCoNi—an alloy widely considered to have a single-phase fcc structure. We observed a delineation between CrCoNi—with hcp as the ground state independent of the local atomic arrangements—and the CrCoMnFeNi HEA, where the magnetic frustration resulting from the addition of Mn breaks a clear trend for relative hcp vs fcc energies. In addition, we showed that there is no driving force for this phase transformation in any other equiatomic ternary derivatives of this HEA. These findings emphasize the fact that high-entropy alloys with more constituent elements are not necessarily superior to their derivatives. Instead, the combination of chemical and, as emphasized presently, magnetic identities of elements govern the properties. An important consequence of this finding is that new alloying combinations can be predicted based on similar favorable magnetic properties. These results provide a new paradigm for design of single-phase alloys with metastable structures through computational guidance and experimental validation.

The observation of the minority hcp phase in the present study is in strong contrast to what has been reported in other microstructural studies on the CrCoNi MEA so far [,,]. The following discussion should point out several difficulties occurring in the identification of the phase, to highlight why the nature of the minority phase could not be entirely explained in this publication and to highlight its general elusiveness. The presence of the phase could be seen in two different as-received material batches that had undergone long-term homogenisation treatment and one batch of the same material that had additionally undergone cold-rolling and subsequent heat-treatment at 800 °C for 1h via TEM. In the last sample, however, no indication of the phase could be found via synchrotron XRD measurement, which is likely due to a lower volume fraction of this minority phase. This is pointing towards the fact that the occurrence of the phase might be strongly tied to processing conditions, especially the cooling rate during production and hence explain why it might not have been present in previous publications on materials with the same nominal composition.

drafts.hypothesis: The differences in mechanical properties during deformation and failure among the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy and its quaternary/ternary subsets are primarily due to changes in stacking fault energy (SFE) and associated local lattice distortions. These structural variations affect dislocation behavior—specifically, the ease of dislocation slip and cross-slip—which in turn drive differences in yield strength, strain hardening, and failure modes.
drafts.material_initial_state: Single-phase FCC microstructures obtained through identical thermomechanical processing of equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
drafts.intervention: Systematically remove one or two elements from the quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy to produce equiatomic quaternary and ternary alloys, ensuring that all alloys undergo the same processing history and are tested under the same deformation conditions.
drafts.conditions: Room temperature tensile tests conducted at controlled (constant) strain rates, with all alloys confirmed to remain single-phase FCC; microstructural evaluations (such as XRD for phase and TEM for dislocation features) are performed post-deformation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Variations in stacking fault energy and the extent of local lattice distortion resulting from the different element combinations.
drafts.mechanism: Elemental removals alter the local atomic size and electronic distributions, which changes the SFE and degree of lattice distortion. In the quinary alloy, a higher degree of lattice distortion favors more extended dislocation cores and enhanced cross-slip, leading to improved strain hardening and ductility. In contrast, the reduced chemical complexity in quaternary and ternary subsets results in higher effective SFE and less lattice distortion, promoting more localized dislocation motion and a tendency toward lower yield strength and strain hardening, potentially increasing brittleness during failure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys are expected to display reduced strain hardening rates, lower yield strengths, and altered fracture behavior (possibly exhibiting more brittle failure modes) due to diminished lattice distortion and increased effective stacking fault energies.
drafts.baseline: The mechanical behavior (e.g., yield strength, strain hardening rate, ductility) of the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies under the strict condition that all compared alloys remain as single-phase FCC structures after identical thermomechanical processing and are tested under similar room temperature conditions. Deviations from these conditions (such as phase separation or testing at extremes of temperature) could introduce different mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a comparative study using identical thermomechanical processing on equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary FCC alloys. Subject all samples to room temperature tensile testing at a constant strain rate while carrying out in-situ high-resolution TEM to observe dislocation dynamics and measure stacking fault formation. Additionally, estimate effective SFE through microanalytical techniques.
measurements: Fracture toughness and mode of failure
Quantitative stacking fault energy (via indirect methods such as electron microscopy or diffraction techniques)
Dislocation structure and dynamics (via in-situ TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the controlled experiments show that the differences in mechanical properties among the alloys do not correlate with the predicted changes in stacking fault energy and dislocation behavior—for example, if quaternary/ternary alloys do not consistently exhibit reduced strain hardening or altered failure modes relative to the quinary baseline, or if similar SFE and dislocation structures are observed across compositions—the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Differences in mechanical properties among the single‐phase FCC equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy and its quaternary and ternary subsets arise because the specific combinations of elements (beyond just the count) lead to variations in local lattice distortion and short‐range chemical order, which in turn modulate dislocation motion and work hardening during deformation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single‐phase FCC alloys processed via thermomechanical treatments; specifically, the Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni (quinary) alloy and its suitably selected equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
drafts.intervention: Systematic variation of alloy composition (removing one or two elements from the quinary) while ensuring retention of a single‐phase FCC structure after identical thermomechanical processing.
drafts.conditions: Ambient temperature deformation with controlled strain rates, ensuring identical processing history and microstructural uniformity across alloys.
drafts.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortion and the extent/distribution of short‐range chemical order.
drafts.mechanism: Variations in atomic size differences and specific chemical interactions among the constituent elements alter the local lattice strain fields and promote differing degrees of short‐range order. These changes modify the barriers to dislocation motion, leading to differences in yield strength and work-hardening behavior during deformation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the quinary baseline, the alloys with fewer elements (quaternary and ternary) will exhibit lower yield strengths and reduced work-hardening capacities because they generate less pronounced local lattice distortion and short-range order fluctuations that are critical for impeding dislocation glide.
drafts.boundary: Results are applicable only to alloys that maintain a single-phase FCC microstructure following identical thermomechanical processing and are tested under the same ambient temperature and strain rate conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the quinary Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy and prepare a series of equiatomic quaternary and ternary alloys by omitting one or more elements, ensuring all alloys have a single-phase FCC microstructure through consistent thermomechanical processing. Perform high-resolution diffraction or advanced TEM analyses to quantify local lattice distortions and short-range order. Subject all alloys to controlled deformation tests (e.g., tensile tests) at ambient conditions to measure yield strength and work-hardening rates.
measurements: Local lattice distortion metrics (e.g., peak broadening in XRD/TEM analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quinary alloy does not exhibit significantly greater local lattice distortion and short-range order that correlates with enhanced yield strength and work-hardening compared to the quaternary and ternary alloys, or if the mechanical properties of the subsets are statistically indistinguishable from the quinary despite measurable differences in lattice distortions, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The enhanced mechanical properties of the equiatomic ternary CrCoNi alloy (and similar quaternary subsets) relative to the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy arise because the absence of Mn eliminates magnetic frustration that otherwise raises the energy barrier for a deformation-induced FCC‐to‐hcp phase transformation. This nano-scale hcp phase, which forms preferentially at stacking faults and twin boundaries during deformation, acts as a structural mediator that enhances strain hardening and ductility.
drafts.material_initial_state: Single-phase FCC microstructures for both the five-element CrMnFeCoNi alloy and its reduced-element (ternary or quaternary) subsets (e.g., CrCoNi) prepared by identical thermomechanical processing ensuring comparable grain size and defect density.
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloys to identical deformation protocols (e.g., uniaxial tensile testing or high-pressure torsion) at controlled temperatures (room and/or cryogenic) and strain rates to activate stacking fault formation and potential phase transformation.
drafts.conditions: Tests performed under controlled temperature and strain rate conditions that enhance stacking fault activity (e.g., cryogenic temperatures or high strain rates) while maintaining similar microstructural features (grain size, defect densities) across samples.
drafts.structural_mediator: The deformation-induced nano-scale hcp phase/lath that forms locally at stacking faults and twin interfaces.
drafts.mechanism: In CrCoNi, the absence of magnetically active Mn removes magnetic frustration, lowering the energetic barrier for the stress-induced FCC to hcp transformation at dislocation interactions (e.g., stacking faults and twin boundaries). The resulting nanoscale hcp regions act as additional obstacles to dislocation motion, increasing strain hardening and prolonging ductility. In contrast, the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy, where Mn induces magnetic frustration, suppresses this transformation, leading to reduced strain hardening and an earlier onset of failure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under identical deformation conditions, the CrCoNi (and similar reduced-element subsets) will exhibit a higher fraction of nano-scale hcp phase formation at defects, which will correlate with increased strain hardening rates, higher yield strengths at large strains, and improved ductility compared to the CrMnFeCoNi baseline.
drafts.baseline: The quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy, which despite having a single-phase FCC structure, shows limited deformation-induced hcp phase formation due to magnetic frustration from Mn.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for alloys processed to yield comparable FCC microstructures and subjected to deformation conditions that readily activate stacking fault formation. It may not apply if additional phases or processing-induced heterogeneities are present that independently affect the deformation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare both equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi and CrCoNi alloys using the same thermomechanical processing protocol to establish single-phase FCC microstructures with similar grain sizes and defect densities. Deform the samples under identical temperature and strain rate conditions (e.g., using in situ high-resolution TEM during uniaxial tensile testing) to monitor for in situ formation of the nano-scale hcp phase.
measurements: High-resolution TEM to identify and quantify hcp phase formation at defect sites (stacking faults and twin boundaries)
X-ray diffraction to assess any changes in phase fractions during deformation
Mechanical testing (stress–strain curves) to quantify strain hardening rates, yield strength, and ductility
Magnetic measurements to compare the extent of magnetic frustration between alloys
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrCoNi alloy does not show a significantly higher fraction of deformation-induced hcp phase or if its strain hardening and ductility are not improved relative to the CrMnFeCoNi baseline under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis that the absence of Mn (and its associated magnetic effects) promotes hcp phase formation and enhanced mechanical properties will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The ternary CrCoNi alloy exhibits superior strength and ductility compared to the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy because the absence of Mn removes magnetic frustration that otherwise suppresses the dislocation‐induced fcc-to-hcp phase transformation. This transformation produces nanoscale hcp regions at defect sites that interact with dislocations and twins, effectively enhancing work hardening during deformation.
drafts.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase FCC microstructures obtained via identical thermomechanical processing for CrMnFeCoNi (quinary), an appropriate equiatomic quaternary subset, and CrCoNi (ternary).
drafts.intervention: Subject all alloys to a controlled thermomechanical processing route (e.g., identical annealing and cold working) followed by tensile tests under the same strain rate and temperature conditions (room temperature and/or cryogenic conditions).
drafts.conditions: Constant processing history and deformation conditions (same strain rate, temperature, and sample geometry) ensuring that each alloy is in a stable FCC state prior to deformation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Nanoscale hcp regions formed along dislocation slip planes and twin boundaries via a dislocation-triggered fcc-to-hcp phase transformation.
drafts.mechanism: In the CrCoNi alloy, the reduced stacking fault energy and the absence of Mn-induced magnetic frustration facilitate a localized fcc-to-hcp transformation during deformation. These hcp regions serve as obstacles to dislocation motion and promote additional strain hardening through interactions with twin boundaries. In contrast, the presence of Mn in CrMnFeCoNi suppresses the transformation, resulting in a different work hardening behavior.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under identical deformation conditions, the CrCoNi alloy will display higher yield strength, enhanced work hardening rates, and improved ductility relative to the quinary CrMnFeCoNi baseline due to the additional strengthening imparted by the transformation-induced nanoscale hcp phase.
drafts.baseline: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi (quinary) alloy processed under the same thermomechanical conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies when all alloys are processed to yield a single-phase FCC microstructure prior to deformation and are deformed under identical strain rates and temperature conditions (e.g., room temperature or cryogenic testing).

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi, CrCoNi, and a quaternary subset using identical thermomechanical processing. Perform tensile tests under controlled strain-rate and temperature (room and/or cryogenic) while conducting in-situ phase analysis (e.g., TEM or synchrotron XRD) to detect any fcc-to-hcp transformation during deformation.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves (yield strength, work hardening rate, uniform elongation)
In-situ microstructural characterization to detect and quantify the formation of hcp regions during deformation
Dislocation and twin boundary density analysis via electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrCoNi alloy does not exhibit significantly higher work hardening or yield strength, or if in-situ analyses do not reveal an enhanced fcc-to-hcp transformation relative to the CrMnFeCoNi baseline, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.
